import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Basic
import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Bounds
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Contracting
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Lipschitz

/-!
# The Pickover/Clifford attractor family

This file formalizes the Clifford map
`F (x, y) = (sin (a * y) + c * cos (a * x), sin (b * x) + d * cos (b * y))`
together with a trapping box, a Lipschitz bound, and — when the Lipschitz
constant is `< 1` — the existence of a unique globally attracting fixed point
via Banach's fixed point theorem.

Note: `ContractingWith` in Mathlib takes a non-negative real constant `K : ℝ≥0`.
Since `cliffordLipschitzConst` is stated as a real number (as requested), the
`clifford_contractingWith` statement uses `Real.toNNReal` to convert it; under
the hypothesis that the constant is `< 1` this coercion is faithful.
-/

open Set Filter Topology Metric

/-- The Clifford map. -/
noncomputable def cliffordMap (a b c d : ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ × ℝ :=
  fun p => (Real.sin (a * p.2) + c * Real.cos (a * p.1),
            Real.sin (b * p.1) + d * Real.cos (b * p.2))

/-- The trapping box for the Clifford map. -/
def cliffordBox (c d : ℝ) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {p | |p.1| ≤ 1 + |c| ∧ |p.2| ≤ 1 + |d|}

/-- A Lipschitz constant for the Clifford map. -/
noncomputable def cliffordLipschitzConst (a b c d : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|))

/-- The Clifford map maps every point into the trapping box. -/
theorem clifford_mapsTo_box (a b c d : ℝ) :
    MapsTo (cliffordMap a b c d) Set.univ (cliffordBox c d) := by
  intro p _;
  constructor <;> norm_num [ abs_le, cliffordMap ];
  · constructor <;> cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( a * p.2 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( a * p.1 ) ) ];
  · constructor <;> cases abs_cases d <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( b * p.1 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( b * p.2 ) ) ]

/-- Bound on a single coordinate of the Clifford-map difference. -/
theorem clifford_coord_bound (a c x1 y1 x2 y2 D : ℝ)
    (hx : |x1 - x2| ≤ D) (hy : |y1 - y2| ≤ D) :
    |(Real.sin (a * y1) + c * Real.cos (a * x1)) -
        (Real.sin (a * y2) + c * Real.cos (a * x2))| ≤ |a| * (1 + |c|) * D := by
  -- Apply the triangle inequality to the difference.
  have h_triangle : |Real.sin (a * y1) + c * Real.cos (a * x1) - (Real.sin (a * y2) + c * Real.cos (a * x2))| ≤ |Real.sin (a * y1) - Real.sin (a * y2)| + |c| * |Real.cos (a * x1) - Real.cos (a * x2)| := by
    rw [ ← abs_mul ];
    grind +splitIndPred;
  -- Apply the bounds on the sine and cosine differences.
  have h_sin_bound : |Real.sin (a * y1) - Real.sin (a * y2)| ≤ |a| * |y1 - y2| := by
    calc |Real.sin (a * y1) - Real.sin (a * y2)| ≤ |a * y1 - a * y2| :=
          Real.abs_sin_sub_sin_le _ _
      _ = |a| * |y1 - y2| := by rw [← mul_sub, abs_mul]
  have h_cos_bound : |Real.cos (a * x1) - Real.cos (a * x2)| ≤ |a| * |x1 - x2| := by
    calc |Real.cos (a * x1) - Real.cos (a * x2)| ≤ |a * x1 - a * x2| :=
          Real.abs_cos_sub_cos_le _ _
      _ = |a| * |x1 - x2| := by rw [← mul_sub, abs_mul]
  nlinarith [ abs_nonneg a, abs_nonneg c, mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hx ( abs_nonneg a ), mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hy ( abs_nonneg a ), mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hx ( abs_nonneg c ), mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hy ( abs_nonneg c ) ]

/-- The Clifford map is Lipschitz with constant `cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d`. -/
theorem clifford_dist_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p q : ℝ × ℝ) :
    dist (cliffordMap a b c d p) (cliffordMap a b c d q) ≤
    cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d * dist p q := by
  refine' max_le _ _;
  · convert le_trans ( clifford_coord_bound a c p.1 p.2 q.1 q.2 ( dist p q ) _ _ ) _ using 1;
    · exact le_max_left _ _;
    · exact le_max_right _ _;
    · exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right ( le_max_left _ _ ) ( dist_nonneg );
  · -- Apply the bound on the second coordinate difference.
    have h_coord_bound : |(Real.sin (b * p.1) + d * Real.cos (b * p.2)) - (Real.sin (b * q.1) + d * Real.cos (b * q.2))| ≤ |b| * (1 + |d|) * dist p q := by
      convert clifford_coord_bound b d p.2 p.1 q.2 q.1 ( dist p q ) _ _ using 1 <;> norm_num [ Real.dist_eq, Prod.dist_eq ];
    exact h_coord_bound.trans ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right ( le_max_right _ _ ) ( dist_nonneg ) )

/-- The Clifford map is a contraction when the Lipschitz constant is `< 1`. -/
theorem clifford_contractingWith (a b c d : ℝ)
    (h : cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d < 1) :
    ContractingWith (cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d).toNNReal (cliffordMap a b c d) := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ ← NNReal.coe_lt_coe, h ];
  · refine' LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul _;
    intro x y; rw [ Real.toNNReal_of_nonneg ( by exact le_max_of_le_left ( mul_nonneg ( abs_nonneg _ ) ( by positivity ) ) ) ] ; exact clifford_dist_le a b c d x y;

/-- The Clifford map has a unique fixed point when it is a contraction. -/
theorem clifford_unique_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ)
    (h : cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d < 1) :
    ∃! p, cliffordMap a b c d p = p := by
  -- By the Banach fixed-point theorem, since the Clifford map is a contraction, it has a unique fixed point.
  obtain ⟨p, hp⟩ : ∃ p : ℝ × ℝ, cliffordMap a b c d p = p := by
    have := @clifford_contractingWith a b c d h;
    have := this.exists_fixedPoint;
    exact Exists.elim ( this ( 0, 0 ) ( by norm_num [ edist_dist ] ) ) fun x hx => ⟨ x, hx.1.eq ⟩;
  refine' ⟨ p, hp, fun q hq => _ ⟩;
  have := @clifford_dist_le a b c d q p;
  contrapose! this;
  simpa [ hp, hq ] using mul_lt_of_lt_one_left ( dist_pos.mpr this ) h

/-- The fixed point is globally attracting: every orbit converges to it. -/
theorem clifford_global_basin (a b c d : ℝ)
    (h : cliffordLipschitzConst a b c d < 1) :
    ∀ p, Tendsto (fun n => (cliffordMap a b c d)^[n] p) atTop
      (𝓝 (Classical.choose (clifford_unique_fixedPoint a b c d h))) := by
  intro p;
  have := @clifford_contractingWith a b c d h;
  convert this.tendsto_iterate_fixedPoint p;
  exact ExistsUnique.unique ( clifford_unique_fixedPoint a b c d h ) ( Classical.choose_spec ( clifford_unique_fixedPoint a b c d h ) |>.1 ) ( this.fixedPoint_isFixedPt )

# Computational Evidence — Pickover/Clifford Attractor Family

## The maps

Clifford map (parameters a,b,c,d):
    x' = sin(a y) + c cos(a x)
    y' = sin(b x) + d cos(b y)

de Jong map:
    x' = sin(a y) - cos(b x)
    y' = sin(c x) - cos(d y)

## 1. Trapping region (basin geometry)

For the Clifford map, every output coordinate is bounded:
    |x'| ≤ |sin(a y)| + |c||cos(a x)| ≤ 1 + |c|
    |y'| ≤ 1 + |d|
So the whole plane maps in ONE step into the box
    B = [-(1+|c|), 1+|c|] × [-(1+|d|), 1+|d|].
Hence B is forward-invariant and the basin of the attracting set is all of ℝ².
For the de Jong map every coordinate lies in [-2,2] (|sin|≤1, |cos|≤1).

## 2. Lipschitz / contraction threshold

Using |sin u - sin v| ≤ |u-v| and |cos u - cos v| ≤ |u-v| with the sup (Prod)
metric on ℝ²:
    dist(F p, F q) ≤ max(|a|(1+|c|), |b|(1+|d|)) · dist(p,q).
So when
    |a|(1+|c|) < 1  and  |b|(1+|d|) < 1
the Clifford map is a Banach contraction → a UNIQUE fixed point whose basin is
the entire plane (every orbit converges to it). This is the "simple attractor"
region of the bifurcation diagram.

Sample threshold values (c=d=0):  contraction iff |a|<1 and |b|<1.

## 3. Bifurcation: loss of uniqueness outside the contraction region

Take a=b=2, c=d=0:  clifford(x,y) = (sin 2y, sin 2x).
Fixed points on the diagonal solve  x = sin(2x).
  * x = 0 is always a solution → (0,0) is a fixed point.
  * h(x) = sin(2x) - x has h(0.5) = sin 1 - 0.5 ≈ 0.3415 > 0,
    h(1) = sin 2 - 1 ≈ -0.0907 < 0, so by IVT there is x₀ ∈ (0.5,1) with
    sin(2x₀) = x₀, giving a SECOND fixed point (x₀,x₀) ≠ (0,0).

Numerical root: x₀ ≈ 0.9477.  (sin(2·0.9477) ≈ sin(1.8954) ≈ 0.9477.)

Thus at (a,b,c,d) = (2,2,0,0) the fixed point is NOT unique — the contraction
threshold |a|(1+|c|)=1 is a genuine bifurcation boundary between
"single global attractor" and "multiple invariant points".

## OEIS / external signals
No integer sequence is central here; the object is a real-parameter dynamical
family (Pickover, *Computers, Pattern, Chaos and Beauty*, 1990; P. de Jong's
attractors). The formalization targets the rigorous trapping-region and
contraction-threshold facts that underlie the empirical bifurcation diagrams.

# Future Directions — Pickover/Clifford Attractor Family

Derived from the verified results in `Catalog/Geometry/CliffordAttractor.lean`
and `Catalog/Geometry/CliffordBifurcation.lean`.  This cycle proved:

* a universal **trapping box** `[-(1+|c|),1+|c|]×[-(1+|d|),1+|d|]` that the whole
  plane enters in one step (`clifford_mapsTo_box`, `clifford_box_invariant`);
* a global **Lipschitz bound** `max(|a|(1+|c|),|b|(1+|d|))` (`clifford_dist_le`);
* a **contraction regime** `|a|(1+|c|)<1 ∧ |b|(1+|d|)<1` giving a unique fixed
  point with global basin (`clifford_unique_fixedPoint`, `clifford_global_basin`);
* **sharpness**: at `(2,2,0,0)` uniqueness fails — two fixed points exist
  (`clifford_nonunique_fixedPoint_at_two`).

---

## Conjecture 1 — Period-doubling beyond the contraction curve
Just outside the contraction curve `max(|a|(1+|c|),|b|(1+|d|)) = 1`, the Clifford
map (with `c=d=0`, `a=b=K`) acquires, in addition to the fixed point at the origin,
a 2-cycle for `K` in some interval `(1, K₂)`, before higher-period orbits appear.

* **The key insight is** that the diagonal restriction `x ↦ sin(Kx)` is a smooth
  unimodal-type interval map whose multiplier at `0` is exactly `K`; the
  contraction threshold `K=1` is the first tangency where the derivative leaves the
  unit disk, the canonical trigger of a period-doubling cascade.
* **Why now?** We have already formalized the threshold and the first
  symmetry-breaking event (loss of uniqueness at `K=2`); the 1-D diagonal reduction
  makes the next bifurcation a finite analytic-IVT computation, exactly the regime
  where the subagent succeeded on `exists_root_sin_two`.

## Conjecture 2 — Sharp trapping box is attained
The trapping bound is sharp: for every `c` there exist parameters and an orbit
point with first coordinate arbitrarily close to `1+|c|`; i.e. the box
`[-(1+|c|),1+|c|]×[-(1+|d|),1+|d|]` is the *smallest* axis-aligned box containing
the forward image of the plane.

* **The key insight is** that `|sin(ay)+c cos(ax)|` attains `1+|c|` whenever the
  phases `ay` and `ax` can be chosen with `sin(ay)=±1` and `cos(ax)=±1`
  simultaneously, which is possible for generic irrational frequency ratios by
  density of `(ax,ay) mod 2π`.
* **Why now?** The upper bound is already a theorem (`clifford_fst_abs_le`); only
  the matching lower/attainment direction remains, reducing the open problem to an
  equidistribution/density statement on the torus.

## Conjecture 3 — Contraction ⇒ exponential basin convergence rate
In the contraction regime every orbit converges to the unique fixed point at a
geometric rate `dist(F^[n] x, p) ≤ C · Mⁿ` with `M = max(|a|(1+|c|),|b|(1+|d|))`,
and `M` is the exact asymptotic rate (no faster constant works for generic data).

* **The key insight is** that the global Lipschitz constant `M` we proved is also a
  lower bound on the local contraction near `p` whenever the linearization has
  spectral radius `M`, so the Banach rate is tight rather than merely an upper
  bound.
* **Why now?** `clifford_global_basin` already delivers `Tendsto`; Mathlib's
  `ContractingWith` packages the quantitative `edist (f^[n] x) y ≤ … * Kⁿ` bound we
  discarded, so the upper rate is one extraction away and only tightness is open.

## Conjecture 4 — de Jong family has the same contraction threshold shape
The de Jong map `(x,y) ↦ (sin(ay)-cos(bx), sin(cx)-cos(dy))` is a contraction (hence
has a unique globally attracting fixed point) precisely when `max(|a|,|b|)·? < 1`
in an analogous product form, with trapping box exactly `[-2,2]²` (already proved).

* **The key insight is** that the de Jong nonlinearity has unit coefficients on both
  trigonometric terms, so its Lipschitz constant is governed by the frequency
  magnitudes alone — predicting a *cleaner* threshold curve than Clifford's, where
  the amplitudes `c,d` enter.
* **Why now?** We have the de Jong trapping box (`deJong_mapsTo_box`); the Lipschitz
  computation is structurally identical to the Clifford one we already verified, so
  the contraction theorem is within immediate reach.

  | empty =>
      simpa using (LipschitzWith.const' (0 : β))

      exact (hf a (Finset.mem_insert_self a s)).add

```

```

* Sub-leading coefficient `a₆ = -(1+2+⋯+7) = -28`.
* The depression shift is `r = -a₆ / 7 = 28/7 = 4`.
* `g := taylor 4 f` has roots `i - 4` for `i = 1..7`, i.e. `{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3}`.
* These roots are symmetric about `0`, so their sum is `0`, hence the `x⁶`
  coefficient of `g` is `0`. ✓ (matches `septic_tschirnhaus`).

The root correspondence `f.eval x = 0 ↔ g.eval (x - 4) = 0` is visible directly:
`x ∈ {1..7} ⟺ x-4 ∈ {-3..3}`.

This is the `n = 7`, `char 0` instance of the general lemma `taylor_depresses`,
whose key computation is that the degree-`(n-1)` Hasse derivative of a monic
degree-`n` polynomial is the affine function `a_{n-1} + n·y`.

## 2. Superposition inner layer as a binary fold

For `n = 3`, `φ = (sin, cos, id)`, `x = (a,b,c)`:

```
innerSum φ x = sin a + cos b + c
             = sin a + (cos b + (c + 0))
             = List.foldr (·+·) 0 [sin a, cos b, c].
```

Every aggregation step uses only the single **two-variable** function `(·+·)` —

**Conjecture.** For every `n ≥ 2` there exist continuous inner functions

The key insight is... the inner functions can be taken **universal** (a single
"address" map separating points of the cube), reducing the existence problem to a
Baire-category / Stone–Weierstrass density argument over a fixed coding map,
which the `superposition` calculus of this cycle already isolates as the target
object.

Why now? This cycle nailed the *algebra* of `superposition` (closure under `+`,
scaling, the binary-fold normal form). The only missing ingredient is the
analytic existence of the universal inner code — a self-contained metric-space
construction, not an open problem.

## 2. Quantitative depth–width trade-off for Lipschitz superpositions

**Conjecture.** The bound `Lip ≤ Σ_q KΦ_q·(Σ_p Kφ_{q,p})` of
`superposition_lipschitz` is *tight* and, conversely, any `L`-Lipschitz function
on `[0,1]ⁿ` admits an ε-approximating superposition whose constant is
`O(L)` independent of `n` (only the width `2n+1` grows).

The key insight is... the Lipschitz constant of a Kolmogorov superposition is
controlled *additively in the inner layer and multiplicatively across layers*,
so dimension enters only through the width `2n+1`, not through the regularity
constant.

Why now? `superposition_lipschitz` already gives the explicit upper bound; the
tightness witness (affine pieces) is computed in `Hilbert13_ComputationalEvidence.md`.
The remaining step is the matching approximation lower bound.

## 3. Second Tschirnhaus rung: removing `a₅` from the depressed septic

**Conjecture.** Every depressed monic septic `y⁷ + b₅y⁵ + ⋯ + b₀` can be brought
to a *doubly* depressed form `z⁷ + c₄z⁴ + ⋯ + c₀` (no `z⁶`, no `z⁵`) by a
quadratic Tschirnhaus substitution `z = y² + uy + v`, with the auxiliary `(u,v)`
solving one quadratic — hence still expressible by functions of **two** variables.

The key insight is... eliminating the next coefficient costs exactly one
algebraic degree of freedom solvable by radicals (a quadratic), so the parameter
count drops `6 → 5` while staying inside the 2-variable toolbox, mirroring
`septic_tschirnhaus`'s `7 → 6`.

Why now? `taylor_depresses` and the `taylor_eval` root correspondence give a
reusable template; the quadratic rung is the same pattern with `comp (X² + …)`
instead of `comp (X + C r)`.

## 4. Sharpness of the width `2n+1`

**Conjecture.** There is a continuous `f : [0,1]ⁿ → ℝ` admitting **no**
representation `Σ_{q=0}^{2n-1} Φ_q(Σ_p φ_{q,p}(x_p))` with only `2n` outer terms
and continuous data — i.e. Kolmogorov's `2n+1` is optimal.

The key insight is... the failure of additive closure at *fixed* width (observed
in `superposition_add`, where adding two superpositions strictly increases `m`)
is the finite-dimensional shadow of a genuine obstruction at width `2n`.

Why now? The cycle made the width-growth phenomenon precise and formal; turning
the qualitative "cannot keep `m` fixed" into a concrete `2n`-impossibility is a
sharp, testable target.

## 5. Algebraic (not just continuous) Hilbert 13 for degree 7

**Conjecture.** The root of the depressed septic, as a function of `(b₁,b₂,b₃)`
after full Tschirnhaus reduction to the 3-parameter Hilbert family
`x⁷ + b₃x³ + b₂x² + b₁x + 1`, is **not** expressible by *algebraic* functions of
two variables (the algebraic analogue remains open), even though the *continuous*
answer is yes.

The key insight is... Hilbert 13 splits sharply by category — `continuous` ⇒

Why now? With `septic_tschirnhaus` formal, the reduction to the 3-parameter

/-
# Pure Nash equilibria of finite potential games as combinatorial fixed points

This file gives a *constructive, combinatorial* existence theorem for pure-strategy
Nash equilibria: in any finite game that admits an **exact potential function**,
a maximiser of the potential is a pure Nash equilibrium (Monderer–Shapley).  The
"fixed point" here is purely combinatorial: it is the argmax of a real-valued
function over a finite set, supplied by `Finite.exists_max`.  This is the
finite-game analogue of "Sperner's lemma ⇒ Brouwer ⇒ Nash": the existence engine
is finite combinatorics rather than topology.

A game is given by:
* a finite player set `ι`,
* finite, nonempty strategy sets `σ i` for each player,
* payoff functions `u i : Profile σ → ℝ`,
where a `Profile` assigns to each player a strategy.  A unilateral deviation of
player `i` to strategy `s` is `Function.update p i s`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "Sperner ⇒ Nash" is, at bottom, a finiteness
--   principle.  For the pure-strategy world it should reduce to: a potential
--   maximiser is a Nash equilibrium, and maximisers exist over finite sets.
-- Experiment (Experimenter): Formalised exact potentials and proved
--   `isNash_of_maximizer` directly from the telescoping potential identity
--   (`linarith`), then obtained existence from `Finite.exists_max` on `Φ`.
-- Analysis (Analyst): The proof needs nothing topological; the only inputs are
--   the potential identity and finiteness of the profile space `(i : ι) → σ i`,
--   which Lean derives from `Fintype`/`Nonempty` instances on each `σ i`.
-- Critique (Critic): Is the potential hypothesis vacuous or always satisfiable?
--   No — the companion file `PureNashBoundary.lean` exhibits Matching Pennies,
--   a finite game with NO pure Nash equilibrium, hence NO exact potential.  So
--   the hypothesis is genuinely load-bearing and the theorem is sharp.
-- Synthesis (PI): `exists_pureNash_of_potential` is the headline; the
--   common-interest corollary shows a natural class where it always applies.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace SpernerNash

open Function

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {σ : ι → Type*}
  [∀ i, Fintype (σ i)] [∀ i, Nonempty (σ i)]

/-- A pure-strategy profile of the game: a choice of strategy for each player. -/
abbrev Profile (σ : ι → Type*) := (i : ι) → σ i

/-- A profile `p` is a **pure Nash equilibrium** for payoffs `u` if no player can
strictly improve their own payoff by a unilateral deviation. -/
def IsNash (u : ι → Profile σ → ℝ) (p : Profile σ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (i : ι) (s : σ i), u i (Function.update p i s) ≤ u i p

/-- `Φ` is an **exact potential** for the payoffs `u` if every player's payoff
change under a unilateral deviation equals the change in `Φ`. -/
def IsExactPotential (u : ι → Profile σ → ℝ) (Φ : Profile σ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (i : ι) (p : Profile σ) (s : σ i),
    u i (Function.update p i s) - u i p = Φ (Function.update p i s) - Φ p

/-
A maximiser of an exact potential is a pure Nash equilibrium.
-/
omit [Fintype ι] [∀ i, Fintype (σ i)] [∀ i, Nonempty (σ i)] in
theorem isNash_of_maximizer (u : ι → Profile σ → ℝ) (Φ : Profile σ → ℝ)
    (hΦ : IsExactPotential u Φ) {p : Profile σ} (hp : ∀ q, Φ q ≤ Φ p) :
    IsNash u p := by
  exact fun i s => by linarith [ hΦ i p s, hp ( Function.update p i s ) ]

/-
**Existence of pure Nash equilibria in finite potential games.**  Every finite
game that admits an exact potential has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
-/
theorem exists_pureNash_of_potential (u : ι → Profile σ → ℝ) (Φ : Profile σ → ℝ)
    (hΦ : IsExactPotential u Φ) : ∃ p, IsNash u p := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp⟩ : ∃ p : Profile σ, ∀ q : Profile σ, Φ q ≤ Φ p := by
    simpa using Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ Φ ( Finset.univ_nonempty );
  exact ⟨ p, isNash_of_maximizer u Φ hΦ hp ⟩

/-
A **common-interest** (team) game, where all players share the payoff `w`,
has `w` itself as an exact potential.
-/
omit [Fintype ι] [∀ i, Fintype (σ i)] [∀ i, Nonempty (σ i)] in
theorem commonInterest_isExactPotential (w : Profile σ → ℝ) :
    IsExactPotential (fun _ => w) w :=
  fun i p s => by ring

/-
Every finite common-interest game has a pure Nash equilibrium.
-/
theorem exists_pureNash_commonInterest (w : Profile σ → ℝ) :
    ∃ p, IsNash (fun _ => w) p := by
  convert SpernerNash.exists_pureNash_of_potential ( fun _ => w ) w ( SpernerNash.commonInterest_isExactPotential w )

end SpernerNash

/-
# The boundary of pure equilibria: Matching Pennies and the role of the potential

`FinitePotentialGames.lean` shows that a finite game with an exact potential always
has a pure Nash equilibrium.  Here we show that hypothesis is *sharp* by exhibiting
the textbook counterexample, **Matching Pennies**, a finite two-player game with NO
pure Nash equilibrium — hence no exact potential.  This is precisely the obstruction
that forces the move to *mixed* strategies and the genuinely topological
Sperner/Brouwer fixed-point argument in Nash's theorem.

We also record the positive boundary case: a **coordination** (common-interest)
game does have an explicit pure equilibrium.

* Players `ι = Bool`; strategies `σ i = Bool` (heads/tails).
* In Matching Pennies, player `false` (the *matcher*) is paid `+1` when the two
  coins agree and `-1` otherwise; player `true` (the *mismatcher*) has the opposite
  payoff.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Pure Nash equilibria need not exist; the canonical
--   obstruction is Matching Pennies, a finite zero-sum game with a best-response
--   cycle (the discrete analogue of "no fixed point" without convexity/mixing).
-- Experiment (Experimenter): Brute-forced all 4 profiles of Matching Pennies;
--   every one admits a profitable unilateral deviation, so none is a Nash
--   equilibrium.  This guided the case-analysis proof of `matchingPennies_no_pureNash`.
-- Analysis (Analyst): The mechanism is a 4-cycle of best responses: whoever is
--   currently unhappy can flip their coin, which makes the other player unhappy,
--   ad infinitum.  No vertex of the strategy hypercube is stable.
-- Critique (Critic): The strongest consequence — and the cleanest adversarial test
--   of `exists_pureNash_of_potential` — is that Matching Pennies has NO exact
--   potential: a potential would *force* a pure equilibrium that demonstrably does
--   not exist.  We prove this as `matchingPennies_no_exactPotential`.
-- Synthesis (PI): Together with the coordination-game equilibrium, this maps the
--   exact boundary between games where the combinatorial fixed point (pure Nash)
--   exists and where one must pass to mixed strategies (true Sperner/Brouwer).
-/
import Mathlib
import NumberTheory.FinitePotentialGames

namespace SpernerNash

open Function

/-- Payoffs of **Matching Pennies**.  Player `false` (matcher) earns `+1` if the
two coins agree, `-1` otherwise; player `true` (mismatcher) has the opposite. -/
def matchingPennies : Bool → (Bool → Bool) → ℝ :=
  fun i p =>
    if i = false then (if p false = p true then 1 else -1)
    else (if p false ≠ p true then 1 else -1)

/-
**Matching Pennies has no pure Nash equilibrium.**
-/
theorem matchingPennies_no_pureNash :
    ¬ ∃ p, IsNash matchingPennies p := by
  simp +decide [ IsNash, matchingPennies ];
  grind

/-
**Matching Pennies admits no exact potential function.**  If it did, the
existence theorem for potential games would produce a pure Nash equilibrium,
contradicting `matchingPennies_no_pureNash`.
-/
theorem matchingPennies_no_exactPotential :
    ¬ ∃ Φ, IsExactPotential matchingPennies Φ := by
  intro ⟨ Φ, hΦ ⟩;
  obtain ⟨ p, hp ⟩ := exists_pureNash_of_potential matchingPennies Φ hΦ;
  exact matchingPennies_no_pureNash ⟨ p, hp ⟩

/-- A **coordination** game: both players are paid `+1` when their coins agree and
`0` otherwise.  This is a common-interest game with shared payoff `coordPayoff`. -/
def coordPayoff : (Bool → Bool) → ℝ :=
  fun p => if p false = p true then 1 else 0

/-
The all-`true` profile is an explicit pure Nash equilibrium of the coordination
game.
-/
theorem coordination_pureNash :
    IsNash (fun _ : Bool => coordPayoff) (fun _ : Bool => true) := by
  intro i s; by_cases hi : i = true <;> simp +decide [ hi, coordPayoff ] ;
  · split_ifs <;> norm_num;
  · split_ifs <;> norm_num

end SpernerNash

# One-dimensional Sperner's lemma (combinatorial fixed-point engine)

Sperner's lemma in dimension one is the statement that a properly two-coloured
path whose two endpoints receive different colours must contain a *bichromatic
edge* (a "door"): two adjacent vertices of different colour.  It is the discrete
shadow of the one-dimensional Brouwer fixed-point theorem / intermediate value
theorem, and the base case of the general Sperner lemma that underlies the
combinatorial proof of Nash's theorem.

We model a Sperner colouring of the path on vertices `0, 1, …, n` as a function
`c : ℕ → Bool`.  The number of bichromatic edges is `flips c n`.  The key
quantitative fact is a **parity law**:

* `flips c n` is odd  ↔  the endpoints `c 0` and `c n` differ.

From the parity law we read off the qualitative Sperner statement: differing
endpoints force at least one bichromatic edge, and in fact an odd (hence
positive) number of them, so the "door count" can never be zero.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The 1-D Sperner phenomenon is governed by a clean
--   parity invariant, not merely an existence statement: the *number* of
--   colour-changes between two points has the same parity as the indicator that
--   the endpoints differ.  This is the discrete telescoping/IVT identity.
-- Experiment (Experimenter): Computed `flips` for several colourings of a path
--   of length 5 with differing endpoints; every value was odd (1, 3, 5, …).
--   This matched the parity conjecture exactly, so we proved it by induction on
--   `n`, casing on whether the last edge `c n ≠ c (n+1)` flips.
-- Analysis (Analyst): The Boolean structure makes the step clean: appending an
--   edge either preserves both the parity of `flips` and the predicate
--   `c 0 ≠ c n` (monochromatic edge) or flips both (bichromatic edge), since for
--   `Bool`, `c (n+1) ≠ c n` is equivalent to `c (n+1) = !c n`.
-- Critique (Critic): Adversarial check — could `flips` be odd yet *no* edge be
--   bichromatic?  No: odd ⇒ positive ⇒ the filtered finset is nonempty, giving a
--   concrete witnessing index `< n`.  We turned this into `exists_bichromatic_edge`.
-- Synthesis (PI): The parity law `flips_odd_iff` is the reusable engine; the
--   existence corollary is the Sperner statement proper.
-/
import Mathlib

open Finset

namespace SpernerNash

/-- The number of *bichromatic edges* among the `n` edges of the path on vertices
`0, 1, …, n`, for a two-colouring `c : ℕ → Bool`. -/
def flips (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((range n).filter (fun i => c i ≠ c (i + 1))).card

@[simp] theorem flips_zero (c : ℕ → Bool) : flips c 0 = 0 := by
  simp [flips]

/-
Appending one edge to the path adds `1` to the door count when that edge is
bichromatic, and `0` otherwise.
-/
theorem flips_succ (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) :
    flips c (n + 1) = flips c n + (if c n ≠ c (n + 1) then 1 else 0) := by
  unfold flips;
  rw [ Finset.range_add_one, Finset.filter_insert ] ; aesop

/-
**One-dimensional Sperner parity law.**  The number of bichromatic edges of a
two-coloured path is odd if and only if the two endpoints have different colours.
-/
theorem flips_odd_iff (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) :
    Odd (flips c n) ↔ c 0 ≠ c n := by
  induction' n with n ih <;> simp_all +decide [flips_succ _, parity_simps]
  cases h : c n <;> cases h' : c (n + 1) <;> simp_all +decide

/-
**One-dimensional Sperner's lemma.**  If the endpoints of a two-coloured path
receive different colours, then some interior edge is bichromatic.
-/
theorem exists_bichromatic_edge (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) (h : c 0 ≠ c n) :
    ∃ i < n, c i ≠ c (i + 1) := by
  induction' n with n ih;
  · contradiction;
  · grind

/-
A robustness restatement: under differing endpoints the door count is strictly
positive (the combinatorial fixed point can never vanish).
-/
theorem flips_pos (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) (h : c 0 ≠ c n) : 0 < flips c n := by
  exact Nat.pos_of_ne_zero fun h' => h <| by have := flips_odd_iff c n; aesop;

end SpernerNash

# Future Directions — Sperner's Lemma, Combinatorial Fixed Points, and Nash Equilibria

This cycle formalised the *finite/combinatorial core* of the "Sperner ⇒ Nash"
program: the 1-D Sperner parity law and existence (`SpernerOneDim.lean`); pure Nash
existence for finite potential games via potential-maximisation
(`FinitePotentialGames.lean`); and the sharp boundary, Matching Pennies, which has
no pure equilibrium and hence no exact potential (`PureNashBoundary.lean`). The
conjectures below extend these verified findings.

## 1. General-dimension combinatorial Sperner via mod-2 boundary counting
**Conjecture.** For a proper Sperner colouring of a triangulated `n`-simplex, the
number of fully-coloured cells is odd, generalising `flips_odd_iff` from `n = 1`.
**The key insight is...** that the 1-D proof is a telescoping *parity* argument
(`Odd (flips) ↔ endpoints differ`), and the higher-dimensional statement is the same
mod-2 boundary cancellation lifted along a "door-counting" induction over facets.
**Why now?** We already have the `n = 1` parity invariant fully formalised with a
clean Boolean induction; the next dimension reuses the identical
`filter`/`card`/parity machinery on facet incidence, so the formalisation cost is
incremental rather than foundational.

## 2. Potential = exactly the games whose best-response graph is acyclic
**Conjecture.** A finite game admits an exact potential **iff** its better-response
relation on the profile hypercube has no directed cycle (the finite Monderer–Shapley
characterisation), and Matching Pennies fails precisely because it carries a 4-cycle.
**The key insight is...** that `matchingPennies_no_exactPotential` was proved *only*
through non-existence of a pure equilibrium, but the real obstruction is the explicit
best-response 4-cycle; turning "no potential" into "has an improvement cycle" upgrades
a non-existence proof into a structural classification.
**Why now?** Both endpoints are already formalised — `exists_pureNash_of_potential`
(potential ⇒ equilibrium) and the concrete Matching Pennies cycle — so the missing
middle is exactly the acyclicity ⇒ potential construction on a finite directed graph.

## 3. ε-equilibria from finite grids converge to exact mixed Nash
**Conjecture.** Discretising the mixed-strategy simplex at mesh `1/N` and taking a
Sperner-coloured fully-labelled cell yields an `ε(N)`-Nash equilibrium with
`ε(N) → 0`, whose limit points are exact Nash equilibria.
**The key insight is...** that the pure-strategy results already pin down the
*combinatorial* fixed point (argmax / fully-coloured cell); promoting it to the
continuous theorem only needs a compactness/limit step, not a new fixed-point engine.
**Why now?** The finite existence skeleton (`Finite.exists_max`, fully-coloured cell)
is verified; Mathlib's compactness of the probability simplex supplies the limit, so
the bridge is assembly rather than invention.

## 4. Zero-sum 2×2 games: pure Nash exists iff a saddle entry exists
**Conjecture.** A 2×2 zero-sum game has a pure Nash equilibrium iff its payoff matrix
has a saddle point (an entry simultaneously a row-min and column-max); Matching Pennies
is the unique (up to relabelling) 2×2 zero-sum game with none.
**The key insight is...** that `matchingPennies_no_pureNash` is the *generic* failure
mode, and the saddle-point criterion is a fully decidable finite predicate amenable to
the same 4-case analysis already used for Matching Pennies.
**Why now?** The 4-profile case-analysis proof pattern is in hand, so the
classification is a finite enumeration over sign patterns, directly checkable.

## 5. Quantitative Sperner: door count lower-bounds equilibrium-search depth
**Conjecture.** Along any monotone best-response path on the strategy hypercube, the
number of "label changes" is bounded below by a Sperner-style parity count, giving an
unconditional lower bound on the length of pivoting (Lemke–Howson-type) algorithms.
**The key insight is...** that `flips_pos`/`flips_odd_iff` already certify that a
sign-changing path *must* contain a door, and counting doors lower-bounds path length.
**Why now?** The parity invariant is formalised and positive; converting "≥ 1 door"
into "≥ (parity count) doors" reuses the same `card` bookkeeping with no new theory.

import Mathlib

open Module

namespace InvariantSubspace

variable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]

/-! ## 1. The invariant subspace predicate -/

/-- A submodule `W` is invariant under the endomorphism `f` when `f` maps `W`
into itself. -/
def IsInvariant (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (W : Submodule K V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ W → f x ∈ W

/-! ## 2. Primitive invariance lemmas

These are proved *directly* from the definition of `IsInvariant`; none of them
refers to any existence statement. -/

/-
The line spanned by an eigenvector is invariant: if `f v = a • v`, then
`Submodule.span K {v}` is `f`-invariant.
-/
theorem eigenline_isInvariant (f : V →ₗ[K] V) {v : V} {a : K} (hv : f v = a • v) :
    IsInvariant f (Submodule.span K {v}) := by
  intro x hx; rw [ Submodule.mem_span_singleton ] at hx; obtain ⟨ b, rfl ⟩ := hx; simp +decide [ hv ] ;
  exact Submodule.smul_mem _ _ ( Submodule.smul_mem _ _ ( Submodule.mem_span_singleton_self _ ) )

/-
If `g` commutes with `f` (pointwise: `g (f x) = f (g x)`), then `LinearMap.ker g`
is `f`-invariant, by the calculation `g (f x) = f (g x) = f 0 = 0`.
-/
theorem ker_isInvariant_of_commute (f g : V →ₗ[K] V)
    (hc : ∀ x, g (f x) = f (g x)) : IsInvariant f (LinearMap.ker g) := by
  intro x hx; specialize hc x; aesop;

/-
If `f` commutes with `g` (pointwise: `f (g x) = g (f x)`), then `LinearMap.range g`
is `f`-invariant, by writing `y = g x` and using `f y = g (f x)`.
-/
theorem range_isInvariant_of_commute (f g : V →ₗ[K] V)
    (hc : ∀ x, f (g x) = g (f x)) : IsInvariant f (LinearMap.range g) := by
  intro y hy; aesop;

/-! ## 3. Derived invariance (only via the commuting-kernel lemma) -/

/-
The eigenspace `ker (f - a • id)` is `f`-invariant, because `f - a • id`
commutes with `f`.  Proof uses only `ker_isInvariant_of_commute`.
-/
theorem eigenspace_isInvariant (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (a : K) :
    IsInvariant f (LinearMap.ker (f - a • LinearMap.id)) := by
  intro x hx; simp_all +decide [ sub_eq_zero ] ;

/-
The generalized eigenspace `ker ((f - a • id) ^ n)` is `f`-invariant, because
`(f - a • id) ^ n` commutes with `f`.  Proof uses only
`ker_isInvariant_of_commute` (after checking the pointwise commutation of the
power, which follows from the commutation of `f - a • id` with `f`).
-/
theorem genEigenspace_isInvariant (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (a : K) (n : ℕ) :
    IsInvariant f (LinearMap.ker ((f - a • LinearMap.id) ^ n)) := by
  -- By definition of exponentiation, $(f - a • LinearMap.id) ^ n$ commutes with $f$.
  have h_comm : Commute f ((f - a • LinearMap.id) ^ n) := by
    refine' Commute.pow_right _ _;
    ext; simp +decide [ sub_mul, mul_sub ] ;
  intro x hx; have := h_comm; simp_all +decide [ Commute ] ;
  simpa [ hx ] using congr_arg ( fun g => g x ) h_comm.symm

/-! ## 4. Headline conditional theorem

Given a single eigenvector, we exhibit a nontrivial invariant subspace.  The
proof takes `W = span K {v}`: invariance is `eigenline_isInvariant`, nonzero is
`v ≠ 0`, and properness comes from the dimension bound.  No existential
invariant-subspace theorem is invoked. -/

/-
**Conditional eigenvector theorem.**  If `V` is finite dimensional with
`2 ≤ finrank K V`, and `v ≠ 0` is an eigenvector of `f` (`f v = a • v`), then `f`
has a nontrivial proper invariant subspace.
-/
theorem exists_invariant_of_eigenvector [FiniteDimensional K V]
    (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (hdim : 2 ≤ Module.finrank K V) {v : V} {a : K}
    (hv0 : v ≠ 0) (hv : f v = a • v) :
    ∃ W : Submodule K V, IsInvariant f W ∧ W ≠ ⊥ ∧ W ≠ ⊤ := by
  refine' ⟨ Submodule.span K { v }, eigenline_isInvariant f hv, _, _ ⟩ <;> simp_all +decide [ Submodule.eq_bot_iff, Submodule.eq_top_iff' ];
  · exact ⟨ v, Submodule.mem_span_singleton_self v, hv0 ⟩;
  · have h_subspace : Module.finrank K (Submodule.span K {v}) < Module.finrank K V := by
      exact lt_of_le_of_lt ( finrank_span_singleton hv0 |> le_of_eq ) ( by linarith );
    contrapose! h_subspace;
    rw [ show ( K ∙ v : Submodule K V ) = ⊤ from eq_top_iff.mpr fun x _ => h_subspace x ] ; simp +decide

/-! ## 5. Optional corollary over algebraically closed fields

This corollary is the *only* place in the file that uses a deep input, and that
input — the existence of an eigenvalue (`Module.End.exists_eigenvalue`) — lives
entirely outside this file.  It is combined with the conditional theorem of

endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space with `2 ≤ finrank K V` has a
nontrivial proper invariant subspace.
-/
theorem exists_invariant_of_isAlgClosed [IsAlgClosed K] [FiniteDimensional K V]
    (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (hdim : 2 ≤ Module.finrank K V) :
    ∃ W : Submodule K V, IsInvariant f W ∧ W ≠ ⊥ ∧ W ≠ ⊤ := by
  have h_eigenvalue : ∃ c : K, Module.End.HasEigenvalue f c := by
    apply_rules [ Module.End.exists_eigenvalue ];
    exact Module.nontrivial_of_finrank_pos ( pos_of_gt hdim );

    ∃ W : Submodule K V, IsInvariant f W ∧ W ≠ ⊥ ∧ W ≠ ⊤ := by
  refine' ⟨ LinearMap.ker f, _, _, _ ⟩;

  · exact fun h => hne <| LinearMap.ker_eq_top.mp h

subspace, namely its range.

theorem exists_invariant_of_not_surjective (f : V →ₗ[K] V)
    (hsurj : ¬ Function.Surjective f) (hne : f ≠ 0) :
    ∃ W : Submodule K V, IsInvariant f W ∧ W ≠ ⊥ ∧ W ≠ ⊤ := by
  refine' ⟨ LinearMap.range f, _, _, _ ⟩;
  · exact fun x hx => by aesop;
  · simp_all +decide [ Submodule.eq_bot_iff ];
    exact not_forall.mp fun h => hne <| LinearMap.ext h;
  · exact fun h => hsurj <| LinearMap.range_eq_top.mp h

The formalized results are classical theorems, so the role of computation here is to
(a) confirm the *sharpness* of the dimension hypothesis and (b) sanity-check the
eigenline construction on concrete matrices.

## 1. Small-case calculations

### Dimension 1 (boundary case — no nontrivial invariant subspace)
For `V = K` and any scalar map `f(x) = a·x`, the only subspaces are `⊥ = {0}` and
`⊤ = K`. Hence there is **no** `p` with `⊥ ⊊ p ⊊ ⊤`. This matches the hypothesis
`2 ≤ finrank` in `exists_nontrivial_invt_of_two_le_finrank`: the result is sharp.

### Dimension 2 over ℂ (headline case)
Every `2×2` complex matrix has an eigenvalue (char. poly is degree 2 over an
algebraically closed field), hence a 1-dimensional eigenline, which is a nontrivial
invariant subspace.

| Matrix `M` | eigenvalue(s) | invariant line (eigenvector span) |
|---|---|---|
| `[[2,0],[0,3]]` | 2, 3 | `span{(1,0)}`, `span{(0,1)}` |
| `[[0,1],[0,0]]` (nilpotent) | 0 (double) | `span{(1,0)} = ker M` |
| `[[1,1],[0,1]]` (Jordan block) | 1 (double) | `span{(1,0)}` |
| `[[0,-1],[1,0]]` (rotation) | `±i` | `span{(1, -i)}`, `span{(1, i)}` over ℂ |

closed) hypothesis is essential: over ℝ it has **no** eigenvector and **no**
nontrivial invariant subspace, confirming that
`exists_nontrivial_invt_of_two_le_finrank` genuinely needs `IsAlgClosed K`.

### Commutant / polynomial kernels
For `M = [[0,1],[0,0]]`, `p(t) = t` gives `ker p(M) = ker M = span{(1,0)}`, which is
`M`-invariant — an instance of `ker_aeval_mem_invt`.

No integer sequence is central to these statements; the objects are subspaces of a
fixed vector space rather than a counted family, so no OEIS lookup applies.

* **Real rotation `[[0,-1],[1,0]]`**: a *true* counterexample to the naive claim

# Finite-Dimensional Invariant Subspaces from Eigenvectors and Commuting Kernels

## Abstract

We give a strictly acyclic formal development, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, of the
finite-dimensional algebraic core of the invariant subspace problem. The central
point of this repair cycle is methodological: every *existence* statement for a
nontrivial invariant subspace is derived only from **primitive invariance
lemmas** together with **elementary finite-dimensional facts**. No existence
theorem is used — directly or indirectly — to prove another existence theorem of
the same strength. This eliminates the circular dependency that flagged the
previous attempt as partial.

All results live in `Catalog/MachineLearning/InvariantSubspace/Basic.lean` and
depend only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and
`Quot.sound` (verified with `#print axioms`). There are no `sorry` or `admit`
occurrences.

## The invariant subspace predicate

For a linear endomorphism `f : V →ₗ[K] V` of a vector space over a field `K`, a
submodule `W` is *invariant* when `f` maps `W` into itself:

```
def IsInvariant (f : V →ₗ[K] V) (W : Submodule K V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ W → f x ∈ W
```

This is the only definition in the file, and it carries no proof obligation, so
it cannot be a source of circularity.

## Primitive invariance lemmas (proved directly from the definition)

These three lemmas are the constructive engine of the development. Each is proved
by unfolding `IsInvariant` and computing; none refers to any existence statement.

1. **Eigenline invariance** (`eigenline_isInvariant`). If `f v = a • v`, then the
   line `Submodule.span K {v}` is `f`-invariant. Any element is `c • v`, and
   `f (c • v) = c • (a • v) = (c * a) • v` is again a scalar multiple of `v`.

2. **Commuting-kernel invariance** (`ker_isInvariant_of_commute`). If `g`
   commutes with `f` (pointwise `g (f x) = f (g x)`), then `LinearMap.ker g` is
   `f`-invariant: for `x ∈ ker g` we compute `g (f x) = f (g x) = f 0 = 0`.

3. **Commuting-range invariance** (`range_isInvariant_of_commute`). If `f`
   commutes with `g`, then `LinearMap.range g` is `f`-invariant: writing `y = g x`
   gives `f y = f (g x) = g (f x) ∈ range g`.

## Derived invariance (only via the commuting-kernel lemma)

From the commuting-kernel lemma alone we obtain the spectral subspaces:

4. **Eigenspace invariance** (`eigenspace_isInvariant`). `ker (f - a • id)` is
   `f`-invariant, because `f - a • id` commutes with `f`.

5. **Generalized eigenspace invariance** (`genEigenspace_isInvariant`).
   `ker ((f - a • id) ^ n)` is `f`-invariant, because any power of `f - a • id`
   commutes with `f` (`Commute.pow_right` on top of the commutation of
   `f - a • id` with `f`).

Crucially, these proofs do *not* reference any theorem that asserts the existence
of an invariant subspace.

## The headline conditional theorem

6. **Conditional eigenvector theorem** (`exists_invariant_of_eigenvector`). If
   `V` is finite dimensional with `2 ≤ finrank K V`, and `v ≠ 0` satisfies
   `f v = a • v`, then `f` has a submodule `W` with `IsInvariant f W`, `W ≠ ⊥`,
   and `W ≠ ⊤`.

   The witness is `W = Submodule.span K {v}`. Invariance is exactly the eigenline
   lemma. Nontriviality (`W ≠ ⊥`) follows from `v ≠ 0`. Properness (`W ≠ ⊤`)
   follows from the dimension bound: `finrank K (span K {v}) = 1` by
   `finrank_span_singleton`, but `W = ⊤` would force this to equal
   `finrank K V ≥ 2`. No existential invariant-subspace theorem is invoked.

## The algebraically closed bridge (corollary)

7. **Algebraically closed corollary** (`exists_invariant_of_isAlgClosed`). Over
   an algebraically closed field, every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional
   space with `2 ≤ finrank K V` has a nontrivial proper invariant subspace.

   This is the only place a deep input enters, and that input lives entirely
   outside the file: Mathlib's `Module.End.exists_eigenvalue` produces an
   eigenvalue (using algebraic closedness, finite dimensionality, and
   nontriviality), and `HasEigenvalue.exists_hasEigenvector` produces an
   eigenvector. Feeding that eigenvector to the conditional theorem of step 6
   completes the proof. The corollary uses only the external theorem and step 6;
   it does not use itself or any later theorem.

   Because Mathlib *does* provide the independent eigenvector-existence theorem
   over algebraically closed fields, we include this corollary rather than
   leaving it out. There is therefore no gap to document on this point.

## Existence from structural degeneracy (kernel/range, not the headline)

For maps that are merely non-injective or non-surjective we give existence
results proved *directly* from kernel/range invariance and elementary facts,
never via the headline theorem of step 6:

8. **Non-injective** (`exists_invariant_of_not_injective`). A non-injective,
   nonzero `f` has the nontrivial proper invariant subspace `ker f`: the kernel
   is always invariant, `ker f ≠ ⊥` because `f` is not injective
   (`LinearMap.ker_eq_bot`), and `ker f ≠ ⊤` because `f ≠ 0`
   (`LinearMap.ker_eq_top`).

9. **Non-surjective** (`exists_invariant_of_not_surjective`). A non-surjective,
   nonzero `f` has the nontrivial proper invariant subspace `range f`, dually,
   from `LinearMap.range_eq_top` and `LinearMap.range_eq_bot`.

## Dependency order and acyclicity

The file is arranged top to bottom so that each declaration depends only on
declarations strictly above it:

```
IsInvariant
  ├── eigenline_isInvariant
  ├── ker_isInvariant_of_commute ── eigenspace_isInvariant
  │                              └── genEigenspace_isInvariant
  └── range_isInvariant_of_commute

exists_invariant_of_eigenvector      ← eigenline_isInvariant            (+ finrank facts)
exists_invariant_of_isAlgClosed      ← exists_invariant_of_eigenvector  (+ external eigenvalue thm)
exists_invariant_of_not_injective    ← ker invariance + ker_eq_bot/top  (NOT the headline)
exists_invariant_of_not_surjective   ← range invariance + range_eq_top/bot (NOT the headline)
```

No existence theorem (steps 6–9) is used to prove another existence theorem. The
constructive invariance lemmas (steps 1–5) are existence-free. This is precisely
the acyclic structure the repair was asked to guarantee.

## Scope

This cycle deliberately treats only the finite-dimensional algebraic core.
Compact operators, the Hilbert-space Aronszajn–Smith theorem, and Lomonosov's
theorem are out of scope and are not formalized here; see `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.

theorem not_dvd_choose_of_prime_dvd {n q : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) (hq : q.Prime)
    (hqn : q ∣ n) (hqlt : q < n) : ¬ (n ∣ n.choose q) := by

    (hq : q.Prime) (hqn : q ∣ n) (hqlt : q < n) :
    ((X + C a) ^ n).coeff q ≠ 0 := by

theorem aks_reverse {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) (a : ZMod n) (ha : IsUnit a)
    (hcomp : ¬ n.Prime) : (X + C a) ^ n ≠ X ^ n + C a := by
  -- Let `q := n.minFac`. Then:
  set q := n.minFac with hq_def
  have hq : q.Prime := by
    exact Nat.minFac_prime ( by linarith )
  have hqn : q ∣ n := by
    exact Nat.minFac_dvd n
  have hqlt : q < n := by
    exact lt_of_le_of_ne ( Nat.minFac_le ( by linarith ) ) fun con => hcomp <| con ▸ hq;

theorem aks_criterion {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) (a : ZMod n) (ha : IsUnit a) :
    n.Prime ↔ (X + C a) ^ n = X ^ n + C a := by
  constructor
  · intro hp; exact aks_forward hp a
  · intro heq
    by_contra hcomp
    exact aks_reverse hn a ha hcomp heq

end AKS

# Computational Evidence — Primality Testing (AKS criterion & Miller–Rabin)

All computations below were run in Lean (`#eval` / `native_decide`) against
Mathlib, and the qualitative conclusions are exactly what the formal theorems in
`AKSCriterion.lean` and `MillerRabin.lean` establish.

## 1. The AKS polynomial criterion `(X+a)^n = X^n + a` over `ZMod n`

For a base `a` coprime to `n`, the identity holds **iff** `n` is prime
(`aks_criterion`). Spot checks for `2 ≤ n ≤ 13`, base `a = 1`:

| n  | prime? | identity `(X+1)^n = X^n + 1` in `(ZMod n)[X]` |
|----|--------|----------------------------------------------|
| 2  | yes    | holds   |
| 3  | yes    | holds   |
| 4  | no     | fails (coeff of `X^2` is `C(4,2)=6 ≡ 2 ≠ 0`) |
| 5  | yes    | holds   |
| 6  | no     | fails (coeff of `X^3` is `C(6,3)=20 ≡ 2 ≠ 0`) |
| 7  | yes    | holds   |
| 9  | no     | fails (coeff of `X^3` is `C(9,3)=84 ≡ 3 ≠ 0`) |
| 11 | yes    | holds   |
| 13 | yes    | holds   |

The failing inner coefficient is always `C(n,q)·a^{n-q}` for a prime divisor `q`,
which is the content of the key lemma `not_dvd_choose_prime_dvd : n ∤ C(n,q)`.

## 2. Carmichael numbers: Fermat liars but AKS-detectable

Fermat's congruence `a^n ≡ a (mod n)` for **all** `a` (a Carmichael number)
fails to detect compositeness. Enumerating `n < 1106` with the Nat predicate
`∀ a < n, a^n ≡ a (mod n)` and `n` composite:

```
#eval (List.range 1106).filter (fun n => n > 1 && ¬ Nat.Prime n && fermatLiarAll n)
-- output: [561, 1105]
```

These are the first two Carmichael numbers — **OEIS A002997** (561, 1105, 1729,
2465, 2821, …). The smallest, `561 = 3·11·17`, is the witness used in
`carmichael_561_fools_fermat_not_aks`:
`∀ a : ZMod 561, a^561 = a` (verified by `native_decide`) yet the AKS identity
fails for base `2`.

Korselt's criterion check for `561` (`n-1 = 560`):
`560 % 2 = 0`, `560 % 10 = 0`, `560 % 16 = 0`, i.e. `(p-1) ∣ (n-1)` for every
prime `p ∈ {3, 11, 17}` and `561` is squarefree — confirming it is Carmichael.

## 3. Miller–Rabin soundness sanity checks

For a prime `n` with `n - 1 = 2^s·d` (`d` odd), every base `a` with `n ∤ a`
satisfies `a^d ≡ 1` or `a^{2^r d} ≡ -1 (mod n)` for some `r < s`
(`miller_rabin_sound`). Example `n = 561` is **not** prime, and base `a = 2` is a
Miller–Rabin *witness*: with `560 = 2^4 · 35`,

```
2^35  mod 561 = 263            (≠ 1)
2^(2·35) mod 561 = 166         (≠ ±1)
2^(4·35) mod 561 = 67          (≠ ±1)
2^(8·35) mod 561 = 1           (a nontrivial square root of 1 appeared: 67² ≡ 1)
```

so `561` is exposed as composite by base `2`, consistent with the field-theoretic
square-root-of-unity argument behind `sqrt_one_in_ZMod_prime`: a nontrivial
square root of `1` can only exist modulo a composite.

## Conclusion

The computational evidence matches the formal results: the AKS identity is an
exact primality test on coprime bases, Carmichael numbers (A002997) are precisely
where the Fermat test fails while AKS does not, and Miller–Rabin never
misclassifies a prime.

/-!
# Gnarl-Preserving Transport: The Edge of Chaos and Reversibility

This companion to `RuckerContinuousCA.lean` studies the *edge of chaos* `κ = 1` of
Rucker-style continuous-valued cellular automata through its sharpest representative: the
**pure transport (shift) rule** on the cyclic lattice `ZMod n`,

```
(shift c) i = c (i + 1).
```

This is the affine rule with weights `(p, q, r) = (0, 0, 1)`, so its gnarl modulus is
exactly `|0| + |0| + |1| = 1`.  We prove that transport **preserves gnarl exactly**
(`gnarl_shift_eq`) — neither smoothing nor amplifying spatial structure.  Hence the
contraction bound `gnarl(step) ≤ κ · gnarl` of the companion file is **sharp** precisely at
`κ = 1`: the inequality becomes an equality for transport.  This is the formal signature of
Wolfram class-4 behaviour: information (a "glider") is moved around the lattice without loss.

Transport is moreover **reversible**: `shift` is a bijection of configurations
(`shiftEquiv`), and on a ring of `n` cells it has period exactly dividing `n`
(`shift_period`), so every orbit recurs perfectly (`gnarl_shift_iterate`).  This is a
continuous-valued, *exact* (period-`n`) strengthening of the Poincaré-recurrence theme used
for boolean elementary CAs in `Computation/WolframCellularAutomata.lean`.

## Research category
Declared as a **cross-domain bridge**: it links the *Computation* domain (cellular
automata, reversibility, Wolfram class-4 transport/gliders) with *Group Theory / Dynamical
Systems* (the cyclic group `ZMod n` acting by translation, exact recurrence, and bijective
dynamics).
-/

namespace GnarlTransport

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ## Definitions -/

/-- First cyclic difference, the local jaggedness of a configuration. -/
def diff (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) : ℝ := c (i + 1) - c i

/-- The **gnarl** (total cyclic variation). -/
noncomputable def gnarl (c : ZMod n → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i|

/-- The **pure transport** rule: shift the whole field one cell. -/
def shift (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) : ℝ := c (i + 1)

/-! ## Basic lemmas -/

theorem reindex_add (f : ZMod n → ℝ) (k : ZMod n) :
    ∑ i : ZMod n, f (i + k) = ∑ i : ZMod n, f i :=
  Fintype.sum_equiv (Equiv.addRight k) _ _ (fun _ => rfl)

omit [NeZero n] in
/-- Transport commutes with differencing: the difference field is itself transported. -/
theorem diff_shift (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) : diff (shift c) i = diff c (i + 1) := by

/-!
# Rucker Continuous-Valued Cellular Automata and the Gnarl Modulus

We formalize a family of **continuous-valued cellular automata** (CCAs) on a finite
cyclic lattice `ZMod n`, in the spirit of Rudy Rucker's "continuous-valued CA" and his
informal *gnarl* complexity measure for the edge-of-chaos regime.

A configuration is a real-valued field `c : ZMod n → ℝ`.  A (translation invariant,
three-cell) **affine local rule** with weights `p, q, r` updates a cell from its left
neighbour, itself, and its right neighbour:

```
(step p q r c) i  =  p * c (i-1) + q * c i + r * c (i+1).
```

The **gnarl** of a configuration is its total cyclic variation
`gnarl c = ∑ i, |c (i+1) - c i|`, a scalar measuring spatial "gnarliness" (how jagged
the field is).  Rucker's heuristic is that interesting (Wolfram class-4) behaviour lives
at the *edge of chaos*: gnarl neither collapses to 0 (order, class 1/2) nor explodes
(chaos, class 3).

The central structural fact (`diff_step`) is that the first-difference operator
**commutes** with the affine rule: differences evolve under the *same* stencil.  From this
we extract the **gnarl modulus** `κ = |p| + |q| + |r|` controlling the dynamics:

* `gnarl_step_le`     : one step contracts gnarl by at most `κ`.
* `gnarl_iterate_le`  : `t` steps contract gnarl by at most `κ ^ t`.
* `totalMass_step`    : the total mass `∑ c` scales by `p + q + r` (a conservation law
                        when `p + q + r = 1`).
* `gnarl_tendsto_zero`: when `κ < 1` the gnarl of every orbit decays to `0` — the rule is
                        in the ordered (class-1/2) regime, with no persistent structure.

The threshold `κ = 1` is the *edge of chaos*; the sharpness of `gnarl_step_le` at `κ = 1`
(realised by pure transport / "gliders") is developed in the companion file
`GnarlTransportReversible.lean`.

## Research category
This target is declared as a **cross-domain bridge**: it connects the *Computation*
domain (cellular automata, Wolfram's four-class taxonomy — cf.
`Computation/WolframCellularAutomata.lean`, which uses the same `ZMod n` cyclic lattice)
with *Mathematical Analysis / Dynamical Systems* (total variation, contraction estimates,
and convergence of orbits).
-/

namespace RuckerCA

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ## Definitions -/

/-- The first cyclic difference of a configuration: `diff c i = c (i+1) - c i`. -/
def diff (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) : ℝ := c (i + 1) - c i

/-- The **gnarl** (total cyclic variation) of a configuration. -/
noncomputable def gnarl (c : ZMod n → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i|

/-- The **total mass** of a configuration. -/
noncomputable def totalMass (c : ZMod n → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i : ZMod n, c i

/-- One synchronous step of the affine continuous-valued CA with weights `p, q, r`. -/
def step (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) : ℝ :=
  p * c (i - 1) + q * c i + r * c (i + 1)

/-- The **gnarl modulus** of a rule: `κ = |p| + |q| + |r|`. -/
def gnarlModulus (p q r : ℝ) : ℝ := |p| + |q| + |r|

/-! ## Basic lemmas -/

/-- Reindexing a sum over the cyclic group by a translation is the identity. -/
theorem reindex_add (f : ZMod n → ℝ) (k : ZMod n) :
    ∑ i : ZMod n, f (i + k) = ∑ i : ZMod n, f i :=
  Fintype.sum_equiv (Equiv.addRight k) _ _ (fun _ => rfl)

/-- Gnarl is non-negative. -/
theorem gnarl_nonneg (c : ZMod n → ℝ) : 0 ≤ gnarl c :=
  Finset.sum_nonneg (fun _ _ => abs_nonneg _)

/-- The gnarl modulus is non-negative. -/
theorem gnarlModulus_nonneg (p q r : ℝ) : 0 ≤ gnarlModulus p q r := by
  unfold gnarlModulus; positivity

/-! ## The key structural lemma: differences obey the same stencil -/

omit [NeZero n] in
/-- **Commutation of differencing with the rule.**  The first-difference operator commutes
with the affine update: the difference field evolves under the *same* `(p, q, r)` stencil.
This is the engine behind every gnarl estimate below. -/
theorem diff_step (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (i : ZMod n) :
    diff (step p q r c) i = p * diff c (i - 1) + q * diff c i + r * diff c (i + 1) := by
  simp only [diff, step]
  have h1 : i + 1 - 1 = i := by ring
  have h2 : i - 1 + 1 = i := by ring
  rw [h1, h2]; ring

/-! ## Conservation law -/

/-- **Mass scaling.**  Each step multiplies the total mass by `p + q + r`.  In particular,
if `p + q + r = 1` the rule conserves total mass — a discrete continuity equation. -/
theorem totalMass_step (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ) :
    totalMass (step p q r c) = (p + q + r) * totalMass c := by
  unfold totalMass step
  rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_add_distrib, ← Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.mul_sum,
    ← Finset.mul_sum]
  have e1 : ∑ i : ZMod n, c (i - 1) = ∑ i : ZMod n, c i := by
    have := reindex_add (fun j => c j) (-1); simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using this
  have e2 : ∑ i : ZMod n, c (i + 1) = ∑ i : ZMod n, c i := by
    have := reindex_add (fun j => c j) 1; simpa using this
  rw [e1, e2]; ring

/-! ## Gnarl contraction -/

/-- **One-step gnarl contraction.**  A single step shrinks the gnarl by at most the gnarl
modulus `κ = |p| + |q| + |r|`. -/
theorem gnarl_step_le (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ) :
    gnarl (step p q r c) ≤ gnarlModulus p q r * gnarl c := by
  unfold gnarl gnarlModulus
  have hbound : ∀ i : ZMod n, |diff (step p q r c) i| ≤
      |p| * |diff c (i - 1)| + |q| * |diff c i| + |r| * |diff c (i + 1)| := by
    intro i
    rw [diff_step]
    calc |p * diff c (i - 1) + q * diff c i + r * diff c (i + 1)|
        ≤ |p * diff c (i - 1) + q * diff c i| + |r * diff c (i + 1)| := abs_add_le _ _
      _ ≤ (|p * diff c (i - 1)| + |q * diff c i|) + |r * diff c (i + 1)| := by
            gcongr; exact abs_add_le _ _
      _ = |p| * |diff c (i - 1)| + |q| * |diff c i| + |r| * |diff c (i + 1)| := by
            rw [abs_mul, abs_mul, abs_mul]
  calc ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff (step p q r c) i|
      ≤ ∑ i : ZMod n, (|p| * |diff c (i - 1)| + |q| * |diff c i| + |r| * |diff c (i + 1)|) :=
        Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => hbound i)
    _ = |p| * (∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c (i - 1)|) + |q| * (∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i|)
          + |r| * (∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c (i + 1)|) := by
        rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_add_distrib, ← Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.mul_sum,
          ← Finset.mul_sum]
    _ = (|p| + |q| + |r|) * ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i| := by
        have e1 : ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c (i - 1)| = ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i| := by
          have := reindex_add (fun j => |diff c j|) (-1); simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using this
        have e2 : ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c (i + 1)| = ∑ i : ZMod n, |diff c i| := by
          have := reindex_add (fun j => |diff c j|) 1; simpa using this
        rw [e1, e2]; ring

/-- **Multi-step gnarl contraction.**  After `t` steps the gnarl is shrunk by at most
`κ ^ t`. -/
theorem gnarl_iterate_le (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ) (t : ℕ) :
    gnarl ((step p q r)^[t] c) ≤ gnarlModulus p q r ^ t * gnarl c := by
  induction t with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [Function.iterate_succ', Function.comp_apply]
      calc gnarl (step p q r ((step p q r)^[k] c))
          ≤ gnarlModulus p q r * gnarl ((step p q r)^[k] c) := gnarl_step_le _ _ _ _
        _ ≤ gnarlModulus p q r * (gnarlModulus p q r ^ k * gnarl c) := by
              apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ih (gnarlModulus_nonneg _ _ _)
        _ = gnarlModulus p q r ^ (k + 1) * gnarl c := by ring

/-! ## Ordered regime: gnarl decay below the edge of chaos -/

open Filter Topology in
/-- **Order below the edge of chaos.**  If the gnarl modulus is `< 1`, then the gnarl of
every orbit decays to `0`: all spatial structure is eventually smoothed out.  This is the
Wolfram class-1/2 (ordered) regime, the strict interior of the gnarl threshold `κ = 1`. -/
theorem gnarl_tendsto_zero (p q r : ℝ) (c : ZMod n → ℝ)
    (hκ : gnarlModulus p q r < 1) :
    Tendsto (fun t => gnarl ((step p q r)^[t] c)) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  have h0 : (0 : ℝ) ≤ gnarlModulus p q r := gnarlModulus_nonneg p q r
  have hpow : Tendsto (fun t => gnarlModulus p q r ^ t * gnarl c) atTop (𝓝 (0 * gnarl c)) :=
    (tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one h0 hκ).mul_const _
  rw [zero_mul] at hpow
  exact squeeze_zero (fun t => gnarl_nonneg _) (fun t => gnarl_iterate_le p q r c t) hpow

/-! ## Sanity: the smoothing 1D heat rule lives in the ordered regime when sub-critical -/

/-- A discrete-diffusion ("heat") rule `c ↦ c + d·Δc` is the affine rule with weights
`(d, 1 - 2d, d)`; its gnarl modulus is `1` exactly when `0 ≤ d ≤ 1/2`, and it is `> 1`
once `d > 1/2` — the classical CFL stability threshold reappears as the gnarl edge. -/
theorem heatRule_gnarlModulus_of_mem (d : ℝ) (hd0 : 0 ≤ d) (hd1 : d ≤ 1 / 2) :
    gnarlModulus d (1 - 2 * d) d = 1 := by
  unfold gnarlModulus
  rw [abs_of_nonneg hd0, abs_of_nonneg (by linarith : (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 - 2 * d)]
  ring

/-- Beyond the stability threshold `d > 1/2`, the heat rule becomes super-critical
(`κ > 1`): the gnarl bound no longer forces decay, matching the onset of numerical
instability / chaos. -/
theorem heatRule_gnarlModulus_gt_one (d : ℝ) (hd : 1 / 2 < d) :
    1 < gnarlModulus d (1 - 2 * d) d := by
  unfold gnarlModulus
  rw [abs_of_nonneg (by linarith : (0:ℝ) ≤ d), abs_of_nonpos (by linarith : 1 - 2 * d ≤ 0)]
  linarith

/-

HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).
